items.readable_text:
Content:
We often want to deal with functions that behave "nicely" on a closed interval:

Content:
- Often, they should be continuous most of the time, and
- any discontinuities should be simple and well-behaved.

Content:
A function [MATH: f(x)] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in [a,b]] if

Content:
- it is continuous on [MATH: [a,b]] except at finitely many points, and
- at each point of discontinuity, the one-sided limits exist and are finite.

Content:
In other words, there can only be finitely many discontinuities, and each of them must be either

Content:
- a point discontinuity (also called a removable discontinuity), or
- a jump discontinuity.

Content:
Note: Every continuous function is piecewise continuous since it has no discontinuities at all.

Content:
Let's consider two examples on the interval [MATH: x \in [0,\pi].]

Content:
- The function
[MATH: {x + 2,|x < 1; 5 − x,|x ≥ 1]
is piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in[0,\pi]] since it is continuous on [MATH: x\in[0,\pi]] except at the point [MATH: x=1,] where there is a jump discontinuity and the one-sided limits exist and are finite:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to1^-}h(x)=3,
\qquad
\lim\limits_{x\to1^+}h(x)=4]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f58d4029fd7d06a567a8d67d0479577b]

Content:
- The function
[MATH: f(x)=2\tan x]
is not piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in[0,\pi]] since the one-sided limits at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] are infinite:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^-}f(x)=+\infty,
\qquad
\lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^+}f(x)=-\infty]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fe30c8eeafd5569ded8f64074167caba]

[MATH: {x + 2,|x < 1; 5 − x,|x ≥ 1.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A function [MATH: f(x)] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in [a,b]] if

  • it is continuous on [MATH: [a,b]] except at finitely many points, and

  • at each point of discontinuity, the one-sided limits exist and are finite.

In other words, there can only be finitely many discontinuities, and each of them must be either a point or a jump discontinuity.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

  • The function [MATH: f(x)] is not piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] since the one-sided limits at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] are infinite: [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^-}f(x) = +\infty, \qquad \lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^+}f(x) = -\infty]

  • The function [MATH: g(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] since it is continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi].]

  • The function [MATH: h(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] since it is continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] except at the point [MATH: x=1,] where the one-sided limits exist and are finite: [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to1^-}h(x) = 3, \qquad \lim\limits_{x\to1^+}h(x) = 4]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: g] and [MATH: h] only."

items.readable_text:
Content:
So far, we have talked about what it means for a function to be piecewise continuous on a closed interval [MATH: [a,b].]

Content:
To define piecewise continuity on a more general interval, we check what happens on every closed and bounded subinterval.

Content:
Suppose [MATH: I \subseteq \mathbb{R}.] A function [MATH: f: I \to \mathbb{R}] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: I] if it is piecewise continuous on every closed and bounded subinterval [MATH: [a,b] \subset I.]

Content:
For example, consider the floor function [MATH: f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor] on the interval [MATH: [0, \infty).]

Content:
- It has infinitely many jump discontinuities at the integers [MATH: x = 1, 2, 3, \dots]
- However, any closed and bounded subinterval [MATH: [a,b] \subset [0, \infty)] contains only finitely many integers.
- Thus, [MATH: f] is piecewise continuous on every such [MATH: [a,b],] so it is piecewise continuous on [MATH: [0, \infty).]

Content:
Note: If a function has infinitely many discontinuities on some closed and bounded interval [MATH: [a,b],] then it is not piecewise continuous on any interval that contains [MATH: [a,b].]

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following functions are piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).]

[MATH: f(x)|= {1,|⌈x⌉is even; − 1,|⌈x⌉is odd; g(x)|= u(x − 1) + u(x − (1)/(2)) + u(x − (1)/(3)) + ⋯; h(x)|= ⌈(x)/(2)⌉] Note that [MATH: u(x)] is the unit step function, and [MATH: \lceil x \rceil] is the ceiling function.

Note that [MATH: u(x)] is the unit step function, and [MATH: \lceil x \rceil] is the ceiling function.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose [MATH: I\subseteq \mathbb R.] A function [MATH: f: I \to \mathbb R] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: I] if it is piecewise continuous on every closed and bounded subinterval [MATH: [a,b]\subset I.]

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

  • The function [MATH: f(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).] The function has jump discontinuities at [MATH: x=1,2,3,\ldots,] and any closed interval [MATH: [a,b]\subset [0,\infty)] will contain finitely many discontinuities.

  • The function [MATH: g(x)] is not piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).] Consider the closed subinterval [MATH: x\in [0,1].] Notice that the function has jump discontinuities at [MATH: x=1,\dfrac12,\dfrac13,\dfrac14,\ldots,] so it has infinitely many discontinuities on this closed interval.

  • The function [MATH: h(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).] The function has jump discontinuities at [MATH: x=0,2,4,\ldots,] and any closed interval [MATH: [a,b]\subset [0,\infty)] will contain finitely many discontinuities.

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: f] and [MATH: h] only."

Note that [MATH: u(x)] is the unit step function, and [MATH: ⌊x⌋] is the floor function.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We often want to deal with functions that behave "nicely" on a closed interval:

Content:
- Often, they should be continuous most of the time, and
- any discontinuities should be simple and well-behaved.

Content:
A function [MATH: f(x)] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in [a,b]] if

Content:
- it is continuous on [MATH: [a,b]] except at finitely many points, and
- at each point of discontinuity, the one-sided limits exist and are finite.

Content:
In other words, there can only be finitely many discontinuities, and each of them must be either

Content:
- a point discontinuity (also called a removable discontinuity), or
- a jump discontinuity.

Content:
Note: Every continuous function is piecewise continuous since it has no discontinuities at all.

Content:
Let's consider two examples on the interval [MATH: x \in [0,\pi].]

Content:
- The function
[MATH: {x + 2,|x < 1; 5 − x,|x ≥ 1]
is piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in[0,\pi]] since it is continuous on [MATH: x\in[0,\pi]] except at the point [MATH: x=1,] where there is a jump discontinuity and the one-sided limits exist and are finite:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to1^-}h(x)=3,
\qquad
\lim\limits_{x\to1^+}h(x)=4]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f58d4029fd7d06a567a8d67d0479577b]

Content:
- The function
[MATH: f(x)=2\tan x]
is not piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in[0,\pi]] since the one-sided limits at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] are infinite:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^-}f(x)=+\infty,
\qquad
\lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^+}f(x)=-\infty]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fe30c8eeafd5569ded8f64074167caba]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Piecewise-Continuous Functions Over Closed Intervals

Example Prompt:
Which of the following functions are piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in [0,\pi].]

[MATH: {x + 2,|x < 1; 5 − x,|x ≥ 1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A function [MATH: f(x)] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in [a,b]] if

- it is continuous on [MATH: [a,b]] except at finitely many points, and
- at each point of discontinuity, the one-sided limits exist and are finite.

In other words, there can only be finitely many discontinuities, and each of them must be either a point or a jump discontinuity.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function [MATH: f(x)] is not piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] since the one-sided limits at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] are infinite:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^-}f(x) = +\infty, \qquad \lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^+}f(x) = -\infty]
- The function [MATH: g(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] since it is continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi].]
- The function [MATH: h(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] since it is continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] except at the point [MATH: x=1,] where the one-sided limits exist and are finite:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to1^-}h(x) = 3, \qquad \lim\limits_{x\to1^+}h(x) = 4]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: g] and [MATH: h] only."

Item 5 — Tutorial: Piecewise Continuity

Content:
So far, we have talked about what it means for a function to be piecewise continuous on a closed interval [MATH: [a,b].]

Content:
To define piecewise continuity on a more general interval, we check what happens on every closed and bounded subinterval.

Content:
Suppose [MATH: I \subseteq \mathbb{R}.] A function [MATH: f: I \to \mathbb{R}] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: I] if it is piecewise continuous on every closed and bounded subinterval [MATH: [a,b] \subset I.]

Content:
For example, consider the floor function [MATH: f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor] on the interval [MATH: [0, \infty).]

Content:
- It has infinitely many jump discontinuities at the integers [MATH: x = 1, 2, 3, \dots]
- However, any closed and bounded subinterval [MATH: [a,b] \subset [0, \infty)] contains only finitely many integers.
- Thus, [MATH: f] is piecewise continuous on every such [MATH: [a,b],] so it is piecewise continuous on [MATH: [0, \infty).]

Content:
Note: If a function has infinitely many discontinuities on some closed and bounded interval [MATH: [a,b],] then it is not piecewise continuous on any interval that contains [MATH: [a,b].]

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Piecewise-Continuous Functions Over Infinite Intervals

Example Prompt:
Which of the following functions are piecewise continuous on [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).]

[MATH: f(x)|= {1,|⌈x⌉is even; − 1,|⌈x⌉is odd; g(x)|= u(x − 1) + u(x − (1)/(2)) + u(x − (1)/(3)) + ⋯; h(x)|= ⌈(x)/(2)⌉]
Note that [MATH: u(x)] is the unit step function, and [MATH: \lceil x \rceil] is the ceiling function.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose [MATH: I\subseteq \mathbb R.] A function [MATH: f: I \to \mathbb R] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: I] if it is piecewise continuous on every closed and bounded subinterval [MATH: [a,b]\subset I.]

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function [MATH: f(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).] The function has jump discontinuities at [MATH: x=1,2,3,\ldots,] and any closed interval [MATH: [a,b]\subset [0,\infty)] will contain finitely many discontinuities.

[IMG: /graphics/d382ac4af0a40eb467736e4be9da14d2]

- The function [MATH: g(x)] is not piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).] Consider the closed subinterval [MATH: x\in [0,1].] Notice that the function has jump discontinuities at [MATH: x=1,\dfrac12,\dfrac13,\dfrac14,\ldots,] so it has infinitely many discontinuities on this closed interval.
- The function [MATH: h(x)] is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,\infty).] The function has jump discontinuities at [MATH: x=0,2,4,\ldots,] and any closed interval [MATH: [a,b]\subset [0,\infty)] will contain finitely many discontinuities.

[IMG: /graphics/a5b2b21c0b5d491bbb537537aec2e88e]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: f] and [MATH: h] only."
